--- title: A Bayesian Workflow format: html: df-print: paged include-in-header: - text: | --- This document walks through a complete Bayesian workflow, from the first question to a result we can defend. Imagine you're in charge of admissions at a large university. You want to know if your admissions process is fair. You've got data from thousands of individual applicants. What now? The workflow starts with a preliminary step, and then has ten steps in three parts. - **Data exploration:** where the data came from, before we ask them anything. 0. **Get to know the data.** Find out how the data came to exist: who is in them, who isn't, and how each variable was recorded. Look at the variables, but not yet at how the outcome relates to the exposure. - **Scientific model:** what we believe about the world, before any statistics. 1. **Ask the question.** Say in plain words what you want to know, and picture what the answer would look like. 2. **Draw the causal model (DAG).** Write down what you assume causes what, based on what you know about the domain. 3. **Define the estimand.** Use the DAG to turn your question into one exact number, before you touch the data. 4. **Simulate the population.** Write a simulation that could produce data like yours. - **Statistical model:** the machinery that turns data into an estimate, tested where we already know the truth. 5. **Write the formal model.** Derive the statistical model from the DAG, in math notation. 6. **Write the Stan code.** Translate the formal model into a program. 7. **Test on simulated data.** Check that the priors imply plausible data and that the model recovers parameters we already know. - **Analysis:** the real data, the estimate, and how far to trust it. 8. **Fit and validate the model.** Run the sampler, check its diagnostics, and run posterior predictive checks. Can we trust the model? 9. **Compute the estimate.** Use the fitted model to estimate the estimand from step 3. 10. **Test its robustness.** How much does the estimate depend on our assumptions? Nothing before Step 8 looks at how the outcome relates to the exposure: here, at how admission differs between men and women. Step 0 looks at the data, but not at that comparison. In principle, you could do steps 1–7 before collecting any data. Step 0 would then be planning how they'll be produced. The steps are numbered, but the workflow is a loop. If the model can't recover known parameters in step 7, or can't reproduce the data in step 8, go back and fix the statistical model. If the result in step 10 depends on an assumption you can't defend, go back further, to the scientific model: the DAG or the simulation. Some failures send us all the way back to Step 0, for example when a result turns out to depend on how something was measured, or on who ended up in the data. Each of those failures teaches us something. This document goes around the loop once: Step 8 finds a flaw in the model, and we go back to Step 5 to fix it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # libraries library(tidyverse) library(cmdstanr) library(tidybayes) library(posterior) library(bayesplot) # Shared helpers for the course decks and pages. Decks load this through # r/deck-setup.R; workflow.qmd includes it directly. # ---- Palette ----------------------------------------------------------------- # Course colors are defined once, in css/deck.scss (the `$brand-name: #rrggbb;` # lines). Read them from there so plots always match the slide theme. read_palette <- function(paths = c("css/deck.scss", "../css/deck.scss")) { path <- paths[file.exists(paths)][1] lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE) found <- regmatches(lines, regexec("^\\$brand-([a-z-]+):\\s*(#[0-9a-fA-F]{6});", lines)) found <- Filter(length, found) stats::setNames( vapply(found, `[`, "", 3), toupper(gsub("-", "_", vapply(found, `[`, "", 2))) ) } PALETTE <- read_palette() BLUE <- PALETTE[["BLUE"]] INK <- PALETTE[["INK"]] RED <- PALETTE[["RED"]] GREEN <- PALETTE[["GREEN"]] GRAY <- PALETTE[["GRAY"]] ORANGE <- PALETTE[["ORANGE"]] TEAL <- PALETTE[["TEAL"]] # A palette color mixed with white: amount = 1 is the color itself, 0 is white. # For light shades (bands, guides) that stay on-palette, e.g. tint(BLUE, 0.2). tint <- function(color, amount) { rgb <- grDevices::col2rgb(color)[, 1] mixed <- 255 - amount * (255 - rgb) grDevices::rgb(mixed[1], mixed[2], mixed[3], maxColorValue = 255) } # ---- Formatting for inline numbers --------------------------------------------- fmt <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",") pct <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%") dollars <- function(x) paste0("$", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")) # z-scores: how many standard deviations each value is from the mean standardize <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x) # ---- Stan index labels ----------------------------------------------------------- replace_indexes <- function(tbl, data, ...) { specs <- rlang::enquos(...) factor_levels <- lapply(data, levels) parse_spec <- function(q) { expr <- rlang::get_expr(q) if (rlang::is_symbol(expr)) { return(list(var = rlang::as_string(expr), dims = NULL)) } if (rlang::is_call(expr, "[")) { var <- rlang::as_string(expr[[2]]) dims <- vapply(as.list(expr)[-c(1, 2)], rlang::as_string, character(1)) return(list(var = var, dims = dims)) } stop("Invalid specification") } parsed <- lapply(specs, parse_spec) out <- tbl for (p in parsed) { var <- p$var dims <- p$dims if (is.null(dims)) { next } idx_pattern <- paste(rep("(\\d+)", length(dims)), collapse = ",") full_pattern <- paste0("^", var, "\\[", idx_pattern, "\\]$") out$variable <- vapply( out$variable, function(v) { if (!grepl(paste0("^", var, "\\["), v)) { return(v) } m <- stringr::str_match(v, full_pattern) if (all(is.na(m))) { return(v) } idx <- as.integer(m[1, -1]) labels <- Map( function(dim, i) { lvls <- factor_levels[[dim]] if (is.null(lvls) || i > length(lvls)) { return(NA_character_) } lvls[i] }, dims, idx ) paste0(var, "[", paste(unlist(labels), collapse = ","), "]") }, character(1) ) } out } # Draw a DAG as a ggplot: a circle per variable, an arrow per direct cause. # edges: c("S -> H", "H -> W") # pos: list(S = c(0, 0), H = c(1, 1), W = c(2, 0)) # labels: full names drawn beside each node, e.g. c(S = "Sex") # above: nodes whose label goes above the circle instead of below # left, right: nodes whose label goes beside the circle instead # highlight: edges to draw in red (e.g. one path); the rest fade to gray # exposure, outcome, unobserved: node names to style dag_plot <- function( edges, pos, labels = NULL, above = NULL, left = NULL, right = NULL, highlight = NULL, exposure = NULL, outcome = NULL, unobserved = NULL, r = 0.3, text_size = 9 ) { ink <- INK blue <- BLUE red <- RED gray <- GRAY nodes <- tibble::tibble( name = names(pos), x = vapply(pos, `[`, numeric(1), 1), y = vapply(pos, `[`, numeric(1), 2) ) nodes$fill <- ifelse( nodes$name %in% exposure, blue, ifelse(nodes$name %in% outcome, ink, "white") ) nodes$text <- ifelse(nodes$fill == "white", ink, "white") nodes$linetype <- ifelse(nodes$name %in% unobserved, "dashed", "solid") nodes$label <- if (is.null(labels)) "" else unname(labels[nodes$name]) nodes$label[is.na(nodes$label)] <- "" nodes$label_y <- ifelse(nodes$name %in% above, nodes$y + r + 0.12, nodes$y - r - 0.12) nodes$vjust <- ifelse(nodes$name %in% above, 0, 1) nodes$label_x <- nodes$x nodes$hjust <- 0.5 side <- nodes$name %in% left nodes$label_x[side] <- nodes$x[side] - r - 0.12 nodes$hjust[side] <- 1 side <- nodes$name %in% right nodes$label_x[side] <- nodes$x[side] + r + 0.12 nodes$hjust[side] <- 0 side <- nodes$name %in% c(left, right) nodes$label_y[side] <- nodes$y[side] nodes$vjust[side] <- 0.5 circles <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(nodes)), function(i) { t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 61) data.frame( name = nodes$name[i], x = nodes$x[i] + r * cos(t), y = nodes$y[i] + r * sin(t), fill = nodes$fill[i], linetype = nodes$linetype[i] ) })) # Arrows run between circle edges, not centers ends <- strsplit(gsub("\\s", "", edges), "->") from <- vapply(ends, `[`, character(1), 1) to <- vapply(ends, `[`, character(1), 2) x0 <- nodes$x[match(from, nodes$name)] y0 <- nodes$y[match(from, nodes$name)] x1 <- nodes$x[match(to, nodes$name)] y1 <- nodes$y[match(to, nodes$name)] len <- sqrt((x1 - x0)^2 + (y1 - y0)^2) gap <- r + 0.04 arrows <- data.frame( x = x0 + (x1 - x0) * gap / len, y = y0 + (y1 - y0) * gap / len, xend = x1 - (x1 - x0) * gap / len, yend = y1 - (y1 - y0) * gap / len, color = if (is.null(highlight)) { ink } else { ifelse(paste0(from, "->", to) %in% gsub("\\s", "", highlight), red, gray) } ) ggplot2::ggplot() + ggplot2::geom_segment( data = arrows, ggplot2::aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend, color = I(color)), linewidth = 1.6, arrow = ggplot2::arrow(length = ggplot2::unit(0.18, "inches"), type = "closed") ) + ggplot2::geom_polygon( data = circles, ggplot2::aes(x, y, group = name, fill = I(fill), linetype = I(linetype)), color = ink, linewidth = 1.2 ) + ggplot2::geom_text( data = nodes, ggplot2::aes(x, y, label = name, color = I(text)), size = text_size, fontface = "bold" ) + ggplot2::geom_text( data = nodes, ggplot2::aes(label_x, label_y, label = label, hjust = hjust, vjust = vjust), color = ink, size = text_size * 0.75 ) + ggplot2::coord_equal(clip = "off") + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous( expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = c( if (is.null(left)) 0.6 else 1.8, if (is.null(right)) 0.6 else 1.8 )) ) + ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(add = 0.6)) + ggplot2::theme_void() } # ---- The three DAG building blocks, drawn the same way everywhere -------------- # fork: X <- Z -> Y # pipe: X -> Z -> Y # collider: X -> Z <- Y # direct = TRUE adds the arrow X -> Y. Other arguments (highlight, unobserved, ...) # go to dag_plot(). fork_dag <- function(x = "X", z = "Z", y = "Y", labels = NULL, direct = FALSE, ...) { dag_plot( c(paste(z, "->", x), paste(z, "->", y), if (direct) paste(x, "->", y)), stats::setNames(list(c(0, 0), c(1, 1.1), c(2, 0)), c(x, z, y)), labels = labels, above = z, exposure = x, outcome = y, ... ) } pipe_dag <- function(x = "X", z = "Z", y = "Y", labels = NULL, direct = FALSE, ...) { dag_plot( c(paste(x, "->", z), paste(z, "->", y), if (direct) paste(x, "->", y)), stats::setNames(list(c(0, 0), c(1, 1.1), c(2, 0)), c(x, z, y)), labels = labels, above = z, exposure = x, outcome = y, ... ) } collider_dag <- function(x = "X", z = "Z", y = "Y", labels = NULL, direct = FALSE, ...) { dag_plot( c(paste(x, "->", z), paste(y, "->", z), if (direct) paste(x, "->", y)), stats::setNames(list(c(0, 1.1), c(1, 0), c(2, 1.1)), c(x, z, y)), labels = labels, above = c(x, y), exposure = x, outcome = y, ... ) } # ---- DAGs that come back in more than one deck --------------------------------- # The surgeon example (weeks 3 and 4): case difficulty decides who operates, and # how it goes surgeon_dag <- function(...) { fork_dag( "S", "C", "O", labels = c(S = "Surgeon", C = "Case difficulty", O = "Outcome"), direct = TRUE, ... ) } # The bedrooms puzzle (weeks 3 and 4): bigger houses have more bedrooms and sell # for more bedrooms_dag <- function() { fork_dag( "B", "A", "P", labels = c(B = "Bedrooms", A = "Living area", P = "Price"), direct = TRUE, highlight = c("A -> B", "A -> P") ) } # print formatting options(scipen = 999) set.seed(1) # plots: a plain theme, and the same color for each sex in every plot theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())) sex_colors <- scale_color_manual(values = c(male = BLUE, female = RED), name = NULL) # a difference in admission rates, in signed percentage points: pp(0.035) is "+3.5" pp <- function(x) paste0(if_else(x < 0, "−", "+"), fmt(abs(100 * x), 1)) # data import df <- read.csv("datasets/berkeley.csv") |> mutate( sex = factor(sex, levels = c("male", "female")), dept = factor(dept) ) ``` ::: # Data exploration ## Step 0: Get to know the data Before we ask anything of the data, we find out how they came to exist. A dataset is not a window onto the world. Someone decided whom to include, what to record and how to record it, and each of those decisions shapes what we can learn. **Where the data came from.** In fall 1973, the Graduate Division of the University of California, Berkeley, made admission decisions for 12,763 applicants to its 101 departments. Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell analysed them in the journal *Science* in 1975.[^berkeley] Our file holds only part of that: the applicants to the six largest departments, labeled A to F. This is the version that is widely shared, and it matches R's built-in `UCBAdmissions` table exactly. We don't have to take that on trust: [^berkeley]: P. J. Bickel, E. A. Hammel and J. W. O'Connell (1975), "Sex bias in graduate admissions: data from Berkeley", *Science* 187(4175): 398–404, [doi:10.1126/science.187.4175.398](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.187.4175.398). The six-department version is documented in R: `?datasets::UCBAdmissions`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # our file, counted the way UCBAdmissions is: one count per department, sex and outcome ours <- df |> count(dept = as.character(dept), sex = as.character(sex), admitted) ucb <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions) |> transmute( dept = as.character(Dept), sex = tolower(Gender), admitted = as.integer(Admit == "Admitted"), n = Freq ) # stops the document if any count differs comparison <- full_join(ours, ucb, by = c("dept", "sex", "admitted")) stopifnot(!anyNA(comparison), comparison$n.x == comparison$n.y) ``` ::: **Who is in it, and who isn't.** Each row is one application to one department, 4,526 in all. Just as important is what the data leave out. - **Only six departments.** The rest of the university isn't here, so our conclusions are about these six. - **Only people who applied.** Anyone who was discouraged from applying, or couldn't afford to, never appears. We'll come back to this in Step 10. - **We can't tell whether anyone appears twice.** There's no applicant ID, so someone who applied to two departments could be two rows. We don't know, and that's worth knowing. **What was measured, and how.** Three columns: `dept`, the department applied to; `sex`, the sex recorded for the applicant (male or female); and `admitted`, 1 if they were admitted and 0 if not. Nothing is missing. Nothing about qualifications was recorded: no grades, test scores or letters. We'll see in Step 2 why that matters. **Who applied where.** How many men and women applied, how each sex's applications spread across the departments, and how selective each department is, counting all its applicants together: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # missing values in each column colSums(is.na(df)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` dept sex admitted 0 0 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # applicants by sex df |> count(sex) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # where men and women applied: each department's share of each sex's applications df |> count(dept, sex) |> group_by(sex) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n)) |> select(-n) |> pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = share) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # each department's size and admission rate (all applicants, not by sex) df |> group_by(dept) |> summarise(applicants = n(), admit_rate = mean(admitted)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Men applied mostly to departments A and B, the two that admit most of their applicants. Women applied mostly to C–F, which admit far fewer. There is one rule for this step: **we don't look at how admission differs between men and women.** That comparison is the answer we're trying to estimate. If we saw it now, we could no longer choose a model for it honestly. Everything else is fair game. With these data the rule is partly make-believe: they're a textbook example, and you may already know how the story ends. With your own data you won't, and the rule is what keeps the analysis honest. # Scientific model ## Step 1: Ask the question Start with the question as you'd say it out loud: *is our admissions process unfair to women?* You don't need technical terms yet. You do need a clear picture of what the answer would look like. A good way to get one is a thought experiment. Take a single applicant and change only the sex on their form. Keep their grades, their letters and the department they applied to the same. Would their chance of getting in change? If it would, the process treats people differently because of their sex. That's what we mean by unfair. We can't run this experiment on real applicants, but it tells us what we're looking for. We'll come back to it in Step 4, where we run it on a simulated population. ## Step 2: Draw the causal model (DAG) A causal model contains no numbers. It's a picture of the variables and of which ones cause which. You'll hear it called a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph), which is a complicated name for a simple idea.
dag { Admitted [outcome,pos=\"-0.619,0.077\"] Department [adjusted,pos=\"-0.858,0.192\"] Sex [exposure,pos=\"-1.059,-0.272\"] Department -> Admitted Sex -> Admitted Sex -> Department }
Sex is the exposure, the cause we're asking about, and admission is the outcome. Department is drawn as *adjusted*: as Step 3 explains, we'll compare men and women who applied to the same department. How do you pick these variables? You use what you already know about the subject. Here, we include sex because sex-based discrimination is a major social issue. We include department because some departments are much harder to get into than others. These are **theoretical choices, not empirical ones**. The data can't tell us which variables we should put in the graph or which way the arrows should point. We make these decisions on the basis of our past experience, previous research, and the consensus of the field. Very different DAGs can fit the same data equally well. The DAG comes from our understanding of how admissions work, and we have to commit to it before the data can say anything. The choices also decide the answer. Every arrow is an assumption, and every missing arrow is an assumption too, usually a stronger one. Together they determine which variables the model includes, which comparison we make, and what the final number means. Suppose we had left department out. The DAG would then say to compare overall admission rates for men and women, and that comparison gives a very different answer from the one we'll get here. Change the DAG and you will almost certainly change the result. The DAG also leaves things out, starting with what Step 0 found the data don't record. Many other factors affect admission. The most obvious is an applicant's qualifications: their undergraduate grades, test scores, letters of recommendation and research experience. Others include how well their interests match a faculty member's, whether they need funding, and how they come across in an interview. A factor that affects admission is safe to leave off the graph only if it's unrelated both to sex and to where people apply. Qualifications can fail on either count. They may differ between the men and women who apply: if women face barriers that only the most qualified overcome, the women who apply are more qualified than the men. And they may affect where people apply: strong applicants may aim for the more selective departments. Since sex affects where people apply too, the men and women who end up in the same department then got there for different reasons, and can differ in qualifications. Either way, because we compare men and women *within* departments, a factor like that can create a gap between them even when there's no discrimination. So we're assuming that, within each department, the men and women who apply are equally qualified. That's a strong assumption, and the data can't check it for us. In Step 10 we'll see how much the result moves if it's wrong. This DAG is not the final word, and no DAG ever will be. There is no "right" model waiting to be found at the end of the process. Every DAG is a simplification. Each one brings some parts of the problem into focus and leaves others out. This one helps us see how department choice can hide or create a gap between men and women. It says nothing about what happens before anyone applies: who is encouraged to apply, who can afford to, and who expects to be welcome. A different DAG would bring those questions into view and push others out. That doesn't mean every DAG is as good as any other. Some fit what we know far better, and the data can rule some out. But the value of this workflow comes from going around the loop: drawing a DAG, seeing what it implies, finding where it fails, and drawing a better one. Each pass shows us something about the problem that we couldn't see before. We never finish. We just understand more each time. ## Step 3: Define the estimand The DAG shows that our plain-language question has more than one meaning. Sex reaches admission along two paths: - A **direct** path, $\text{Sex} \to \text{Admitted}$: departments treat women differently from men who apply to the same department. - An **indirect** path, $\text{Sex} \to \text{Department} \to \text{Admitted}$: women apply to different departments, and those departments admit fewer people. Suppose women are admitted at a lower rate overall. That gap could come from either path, and each one calls for a different fix. So "is admissions unfair?" is still too vague to estimate. We have to choose which path we're asking about. We choose based on what we're responsible for, not on what's easiest to estimate. As the admissions office, we control the decisions departments make, so we'll focus on the direct path. This is the thought experiment from Step 1: change the applicant's sex and keep their department the same. Written as a number to estimate, it's the **estimand**: > **Estimand:** for each applicant, how much their chance of admission would change if > the department saw them as a woman rather than as a man, with everything else about > them, their department included, left as it is; averaged over all applicants. We'll measure it as a difference in admission rates. For example, a result of −0.05 would mean that being seen as a woman lowers an applicant's chance of admission by 5 percentage points. "Averaged over all applicants" is a choice too. It counts each department in proportion to how many people apply to it. We could instead average over the women who applied. That asks what the process did to the women who actually came, rather than how it treats applicants in general, and it counts departments C–F, where most women applied, much more. If every department treats women the same way, the two versions give the same number. If departments differ, they can give very different numbers, so we choose now, before the data can tempt us. As the admissions office, we're responsible for how the process treats everyone who applies, so we average over all applicants. Comparing applicants to the same department means we have to **condition on department**, so department has to go into the model. Settling the estimand before we write any code tells us what the model has to include and what we'll compute from it at the end. ## Step 4: Simulate the population Before writing a statistical model, we write a *generative* one: a simulation that follows the DAG and produces fake applicants. This makes us state precisely how we think the data come about. Later, it gives us data where we know the right answer. The simulation's default numbers come from the tables in Step 0: where men and women applied, and each department's admission rate for all its applicants together. Neither shows how admission differs between men and women. (A stricter rule would rule out even the departments' admission rates, and we'd have to make them up. We've drawn the line at the comparison we're trying to estimate.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Each assumption is an argument, with a default based on the real data. Change them to # simulate a different world. discrimination, admit_rate, male_pref and female_pref give # one value per department, in the order of depts, or a single value for all of them: # admit_rate = 0.4 means every department admits 40%. simulate_admissions <- function( n = 4500, discrimination = 0, # Sex -> Admitted: effect of being female, in log-odds depts = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"), admit_rate = c(0.65, 0.60, 0.35, 0.33, 0.25, 0.07), # Department -> Admitted male_pref = c(0.31, 0.21, 0.12, 0.15, 0.07, 0.14), # Sex -> Department female_pref = c(0.06, 0.02, 0.32, 0.20, 0.21, 0.19) # Sex -> Department ) { # one row per department (single values are recycled to every department) departments <- tibble( dept = fct(depts), discrimination, admit_rate, male_pref, female_pref ) # Sex: 60% men, as in the real data sex <- sample(fct(c("male", "female")), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)) # Sex -> Department dept <- if_else( sex == "female", sample(departments$dept, n, replace = TRUE, prob = departments$female_pref), sample(departments$dept, n, replace = TRUE, prob = departments$male_pref) ) # Department, Sex -> Admitted d <- match(dept, departments$dept) dept_rate <- departments$admit_rate[d] dept_discrimination <- departments$discrimination[d] log_odds <- qlogis(dept_rate) + dept_discrimination * (sex == "female") admitted <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(log_odds)) tibble(dept, sex, dept_rate, dept_discrimination, admitted) } ``` ::: Let's simulate a world with **no discrimination at all**: within every department, men and women are admitted at the same rate. Women just tend to apply to more selective departments. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sim_fair <- simulate_admissions(discrimination = 0) # overall admission rates by sex sim_fair |> group_by(sex) |> summarise(applicants = n(), admit_rate = mean(admitted)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Women are admitted much less often overall, even though the simulation contains no discrimination. The whole gap comes from the indirect path through department. This is why the estimand has to be defined within departments, and why department belongs in the model. If we compared overall rates, we'd find a gap that isn't there. ### Exploring other worlds Every assumption in the simulation is an argument we can change. That lets us ask "what if?" questions about how the gap arises. Here we keep discrimination at zero and change one assumption at a time: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} worlds <- list( "Our assumptions" = sim_fair, "Everyone applies evenly to every department" = simulate_admissions( male_pref = 1, female_pref = 1 ), "Every department admits 40%" = simulate_admissions(admit_rate = 0.4) ) # overall admission rates by sex in each world worlds |> bind_rows(.id = "world") |> group_by(world, sex) |> summarise(admit_rate = mean(admitted)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = admit_rate) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: The overall gap disappears in both new worlds. It needs two things at once: men and women applying to different departments, *and* departments that differ in how selective they are. Remove either one and the gap goes away. Try other values yourself. What happens if women prefer the *least* selective departments? What if one department admits almost everyone? What if only one department discriminates (`discrimination = c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)`)? We'll need that last one in Step 8. # Statistical model ## Step 5: Write the formal model Next, we turn the DAG into a statistical model: $$ \begin{align} \text{admitted}_i &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i) \\ \mathrm{logit}(p_i) &= \alpha + \beta_{\mathrm{sex}[i]} + \gamma_{\mathrm{dept}[i]} \\ \alpha &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1.5) \\ \beta_{\mathrm{sex}} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1) \\ \gamma_{\mathrm{dept}} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1) \\ 0 &= \textstyle\sum_{\mathrm{sex}} \beta = \sum_{\mathrm{dept}} \gamma \end{align} $$ It looks complicated, but it has four parts: 1. A **likelihood** (line 1): how randomness enters. Each applicant is admitted or not. 2. A **linear predictor** (line 2): how the arrows in the DAG combine. There's a baseline $\alpha$, a sex effect $\beta$, and a department effect $\gamma$. 3. **Priors** (lines 3–5): what we believe before we see the data. 4. **Constraints** (line 6): each set of effects adds up to zero. Without this, the model couldn't tell its parts apart. Adding 1 to $\alpha$ and subtracting 1 from every $\gamma$ would give exactly the same predictions. With the constraint, $\alpha$ is the overall average and every other term is a deviation from it. Each term in the model matches a piece of the DAG. Sex and department both point into admission, so both appear in the linear predictor. The estimand from Step 3 comes from $\beta$, the term that lets women's and men's chances differ within a department. The model also makes a simplifying assumption: the sex effect $\beta$ is the same in every department. That keeps the model small. We'll find out in Step 8 whether the data go along with it. ## Step 6: Write the Stan code Now we translate the formal model into a program the computer can run: ```{.stan filename="models/berkeley.stan" code-line-numbers="true"} functions { // adjustment for sum_to_zero_vector[K] SDs real stz_correction(int K) { return inv_sqrt(1 - inv(K)); } } data { // prior predictive toggle (skips likelihood calculations) int prior_only; // prior scales real alpha_sd; real beta_sd; real gamma_sd; // dimensions int n; int n_sex; int n_dept; // group indices array[n] int sex; array[n] int dept; // observed outcomes array[n] int admitted; } parameters { real alpha; sum_to_zero_vector[n_sex] beta; sum_to_zero_vector[n_dept] gamma; } model { alpha ~ normal(0, alpha_sd); beta ~ normal(0, beta_sd * stz_correction(n_sex)); gamma ~ normal(0, gamma_sd * stz_correction(n_dept)); vector[n] eta = alpha + beta[sex] + gamma[dept]; if (!prior_only) admitted ~ bernoulli_logit(eta); } generated quantities { // admission probability for every sex x department cell matrix[n_sex, n_dept] p; for (s in 1 : n_sex) for (d in 1 : n_dept) p[s, d] = inv_logit(alpha + beta[s] + gamma[d]); } ``` A few details: - The priors' scales (`alpha_sd`, `beta_sd`, `gamma_sd`) come in as data, so we can change a prior without editing the model. We'll do that in Step 10. - Stan enforces the constraints with `sum_to_zero_vector`. Forcing effects to sum to zero shrinks their spread, so the code widens each prior's scale to compensate. That way, each effect's prior matches the formal model. - The `prior_only` switch skips the likelihood. With it on, the model samples from the priors alone, which is what we need for prior predictive checks. - `generated quantities` reports the admission probability for every sex × department cell. We'll compute the estimand from these. We compile the model and write a small helper so every fit in this document uses the same settings: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} berkeley <- cmdstan_model("models/berkeley.stan", dir = ".stancache") # the prior scales from the formal model priors <- list(alpha_sd = 1.5, beta_sd = 1, gamma_sd = 1) fit_model <- function(data, model = berkeley, prior = priors, prior_only = 0) { data |> select(dept, sex, admitted) |> compose_data() |> c(list(prior_only = prior_only), prior) |> model$sample( seed = 2026, parallel_chains = 4, # run the four chains at once adapt_delta = 0.95, # smaller steps, for the tricky geometry of Step 8's second model refresh = 0, show_messages = FALSE ) } # the estimand from Step 3, computed for every posterior draw: the female − male # difference in each department, averaged over the applicants in weight_by direct_effect <- function(fit, data = df, weight_by = data) { weights <- weight_by |> count(dept, .drop = FALSE) |> mutate(w = n / sum(n)) |> pull(w) fit |> spread_draws(p[sex, dept]) |> mutate(sex = levels(data$sex)[sex]) |> pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = p) |> mutate(w = weights[dept]) |> group_by(.draw) |> summarise(direct_effect = sum(w * (female - male))) } ``` ::: ## Step 7: Test on simulated data We test the model on data where we already know the answer before we trust it on data where we don't. There are two checks. ### Prior predictive check First, do the priors imply plausible data? We run the model with `prior_only = 1` and look at the admission rates it expects before seeing any data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_prior <- fit_model(df, prior_only = 1) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_prior |> spread_draws(p[sex, dept]) |> ggplot(aes(x = p)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = BLUE, color = "white") + labs( x = "Admission probability for a sex × department cell", y = "Prior draws", title = "What the priors imply about admission rates" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/prior_predictive_plot-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} direct_effect(fit_prior) |> ggplot(aes(x = direct_effect)) + stat_halfeye(fill = BLUE) + labs( x = "Direct effect (female − male)", y = NULL, title = "Prior on the estimand" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/prior_predictive_plot-2.png){width=672} ::: ::: The prior on the direct effect is centered on zero, so it doesn't assume discrimination in either direction. It's also wide: gaps of 50 percentage points or more either way are allowed. The admission rates show a problem. The priors pile up near 0% and 100%. That happens because three Normal priors add up on the log-odds scale, and a log-odds of ±3 is already 5% or 95%. These priors are looser than our actual knowledge: we don't believe departments admit nearly everyone or nearly no one. This is a judgment call. We could tighten $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ now. With thousands of applicants, we expect the data to outweigh the priors, so we'll keep them and check that expectation directly in Step 10, by refitting with those priors half and twice as wide. ### Parameter recovery Second, can the model find an effect we put there ourselves? We simulate three populations: one with no discrimination, one where women are penalized by 0.5 on the log-odds scale, and one where they're penalized by 1. We fit the model to each and check whether the posterior covers the true value of the estimand. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # the true value of the estimand: switch each simulated applicant's sex, keep everything # else the same, and average the change in their chance of admission true_direct_effect <- function(sim) { log_odds_male <- qlogis(sim$dept_rate) log_odds_female <- log_odds_male + sim$dept_discrimination mean(plogis(log_odds_female) - plogis(log_odds_male)) } recovery <- tibble(discrimination = c(0, -0.5, -1)) |> mutate( sim = map(discrimination, \(b) simulate_admissions(discrimination = b)), truth = map_dbl(sim, true_direct_effect), estimate = map(sim, \(s) direct_effect(fit_model(s), data = s)) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} recovery |> select(discrimination, truth, estimate) |> unnest(estimate) |> ggplot(aes(x = direct_effect, y = factor(discrimination))) + stat_halfeye(fill = BLUE) + geom_point( data = distinct(recovery, discrimination, truth), aes(x = truth), color = RED, shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.5 ) + labs( x = "Direct effect (female − male)", y = "Discrimination built into the simulation (log-odds)", title = "Can the model recover a known effect?", subtitle = "Red ×: the true value of the estimand" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/recovery_plot-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: In each case, the true value falls within the posterior, though at −0.5 it sits in the tail. The model and the estimand code work, at least in a world that matches our assumptions. If they didn't, we'd have a bug or an identification problem, and we'd fix it here, where we know the right answer. Any single simulated dataset is noisy, so a more thorough version of this check repeats it many times with random true values. That's called *simulation-based calibration*. # Analysis ## Step 8: Fit and validate the model Now we fit the model to the real data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit <- fit_model(df) ``` ::: ### Sampler diagnostics Before we look at any results, we check whether the sampler worked. Divergent transitions mean the sampler hit geometry it couldn't explore. $\hat{R}$ should be very close to 1, which means the chains agree with each other. Effective sample size (ESS) should be in the hundreds or more. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit$diagnostic_summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $num_divergent [1] 0 0 0 0 $num_max_treedepth [1] 0 0 0 0 $ebfmi [1] 0.9597315 1.0484008 0.9575626 1.0382318 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fit$draws() |> subset_draws(variable = c("alpha", "beta", "gamma")) |> summarise_draws() |> replace_indexes(df, beta[sex], gamma[dept]) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 9 × 10 variable mean median sd mad q5 q95 rhat ess_bulk 1 alpha -0.641 -0.639 0.0396 0.0387 -0.707 -0.577 1.00 3442. 2 beta[male] -0.0462 -0.0459 0.0407 0.0412 -0.115 0.0192 1.00 3411. 3 beta[female] 0.0462 0.0459 0.0407 0.0412 -0.0192 0.115 1.00 3411. 4 gamma[A] 1.27 1.27 0.0724 0.0713 1.15 1.39 1.00 4379. 5 gamma[B] 1.22 1.22 0.0872 0.0874 1.07 1.36 1.000 3476. 6 gamma[C] 0.00878 0.00725 0.0739 0.0746 -0.110 0.129 1.000 4781. 7 gamma[D] -0.0220 -0.0210 0.0731 0.0717 -0.144 0.0996 1.00 5367. 8 gamma[E] -0.464 -0.464 0.0908 0.0896 -0.615 -0.312 1.00 4718. 9 gamma[F] -2.01 -2.01 0.127 0.130 -2.22 -1.80 1.00 3966. ess_tail 1 2970. 2 2926. 3 2926. 4 3016. 5 3100. 6 3180. 7 2956. 8 2988. 9 2908. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mcmc_trace(fit$draws(c("alpha", "beta", "gamma"))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/diagnostics-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The trace plots should look like "fuzzy caterpillars": chains that overlap and wander around the same region with no trends. ### Posterior predictive check Can the fitted model reproduce the data it was fit to? For each posterior draw, we simulate a new set of admissions for every sex × department cell and compare the result to what we actually observed. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # simulated admissions for every sex × department cell, one set per posterior draw predict_cells <- function(fit, data = df) { fit |> spread_draws(p[sex, dept]) |> mutate( sex = factor(levels(data$sex)[sex], levels = levels(data$sex)), dept = factor(levels(data$dept)[dept], levels = levels(data$dept)) ) |> left_join(count(data, sex, dept, name = "applicants"), by = c("sex", "dept")) |> mutate(admitted = rbinom(n(), applicants, p)) } # what we observed, in each cell and overall cells <- df |> group_by(sex, dept) |> summarise(applicants = n(), observed = mean(admitted), .groups = "drop") overall <- df |> group_by(sex) |> summarise(observed = mean(admitted)) # predicted (intervals) and observed (×) admission rates in every cell ppc_plot <- function(fit, title) { predict_cells(fit) |> mutate(predicted = admitted / applicants) |> ggplot(aes(x = dept, y = predicted, color = sex)) + stat_pointinterval( position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), .width = c(0.5, 0.9) ) + geom_point( data = cells, aes(y = observed), shape = 4, size = 3, stroke = 1.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5) ) + sex_colors + labs( x = "Department", y = "Admission rate", title = title, subtitle = "Intervals: model predictions. ×: observed rates." ) } ``` ::: First, the pattern that started all this: the overall gap between men and women, ignoring department. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} predict_cells(fit) |> group_by(.draw, sex) |> summarise(predicted = sum(admitted) / sum(applicants), .groups = "drop") |> ggplot(aes(x = predicted, y = sex, color = sex)) + stat_pointinterval(.width = c(0.5, 0.9)) + geom_point(data = overall, aes(x = observed), shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.5) + sex_colors + labs( x = "Overall admission rate", y = NULL, title = "Posterior predictive check: the overall gap", subtitle = "Intervals: model predictions. ×: observed rates." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/ppc_overall-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Overall, 45% of men and 30% of women were admitted. The model reproduces that gap, even though its sex effect is small: as in the Step 4 simulation, the gap comes from where men and women apply. Now the same check, department by department: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ppc_plot(fit, "Posterior predictive check: one sex effect for all departments") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/ppc-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: For most departments, the observed rates (×) fall inside the predicted intervals. Department A is the exception. Women there are admitted 82% of the time, against 62% of men, well above anything the model predicts. The model can't capture this because in Step 5 we assumed the sex effect is the same in every department, and department A breaks that pattern. This is the posterior predictive check doing its job. It tells us exactly where the model is too simple. And here the misfit matters for the answer, not just for the picture. The estimand averages each department's own female − male difference. A model that forces those differences to be equal doesn't average them: it compromises between them, leaning toward the departments where both sexes applied in numbers. Department A, with many men but only 108 women, gets less say in that compromise than the estimand gives it. So we go back around the loop. ## Steps 5–8 again: a sex effect for each department ### Step 5: Let the sex effect vary The new model gives each department its own sex effect: $$ \begin{align} \text{admitted}_i &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_i) \\ \mathrm{logit}(p_i) &= \alpha + \beta_{\mathrm{sex}[i],\,\mathrm{dept}[i]} + \gamma_{\mathrm{dept}[i]} \\ \beta_{\mathrm{sex},\,\mathrm{dept}} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(\bar\beta_{\mathrm{sex}}, \tau) \\ \bar\beta_{\mathrm{sex}} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1) \\ \tau &\sim \mathrm{Half\text{-}Normal}(0, 0.5) \\ \alpha &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1.5) \\ \gamma_{\mathrm{dept}} &\sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, 1) \\ 0 &= \textstyle\sum_{\mathrm{sex}} \bar\beta = \sum_{\mathrm{sex}} \beta_{\cdot,\,\mathrm{dept}} = \sum_{\mathrm{dept}} \gamma \end{align} $$ The departments' sex effects aren't unrelated: they're drawn from one distribution, around an average effect $\bar\beta$ (the old $\beta$) with spread $\tau$. The model learns $\tau$ from the data. If departments treat women alike, $\tau$ is near zero and we're back to the first model. If they don't, each department's effect is estimated mostly from its own applicants. A department with few applicants of one sex, like B with its 25 women, is pulled toward the average. This is *partial pooling*: it lets departments differ without chasing the noise in small groups. The prior on $\tau$ says the departments' effects probably differ by a few tenths on the log-odds scale, and rarely by more than one. ### Step 6: The Stan code ```{.stan filename="models/berkeley_varying.stan" code-line-numbers="true"} // berkeley.stan, with a sex effect that varies by department functions { // adjustment for sum_to_zero_vector[K] SDs real stz_correction(int K) { return inv_sqrt(1 - inv(K)); } } data { // prior predictive toggle (skips likelihood calculations) int prior_only; // prior scales real alpha_sd; real beta_sd; real tau_sd; real gamma_sd; // dimensions int n; int n_sex; int n_dept; // group indices array[n] int sex; array[n] int dept; // observed outcomes array[n] int admitted; } transformed data { // each applicant's sex x department cell, as a position in to_vector(beta) array[n] int cell; for (i in 1 : n) cell[i] = sex[i] + n_sex * (dept[i] - 1); } parameters { real alpha; sum_to_zero_vector[n_sex] beta_bar; // average sex effect real tau; // how much the sex effect varies between departments array[n_dept] sum_to_zero_vector[n_sex] z; // each department's deviation, in units of tau sum_to_zero_vector[n_dept] gamma; } transformed parameters { // sex effect in each department: beta[s, d] matrix[n_sex, n_dept] beta; for (d in 1 : n_dept) beta[ : , d] = beta_bar + tau * z[d]; } model { alpha ~ normal(0, alpha_sd); beta_bar ~ normal(0, beta_sd * stz_correction(n_sex)); tau ~ normal(0, tau_sd); for (d in 1 : n_dept) z[d] ~ normal(0, stz_correction(n_sex)); gamma ~ normal(0, gamma_sd * stz_correction(n_dept)); vector[n] eta = alpha + to_vector(beta)[cell] + gamma[dept]; if (!prior_only) admitted ~ bernoulli_logit(eta); } generated quantities { // admission probability for every sex x department cell matrix[n_sex, n_dept] p; for (s in 1 : n_sex) for (d in 1 : n_dept) p[s, d] = inv_logit(alpha + beta[s, d] + gamma[d]); } ``` - `beta` is now a matrix with a column for each department, built as `beta_bar + tau * z`. The sampler explores `z`, which is standard Normal, rather than `beta` itself. This is the same model written in a form that is easier to sample when $\tau$ is small (a *non-centered* parameterization). - `cell`, in `transformed data`, is each applicant's position in `beta` once its columns are stacked into one vector. It lets the linear predictor pick each applicant's sex effect in one line, like `gamma[dept]`. - `p` is the same sex × department matrix as before, so `direct_effect()` works unchanged. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} varying <- cmdstan_model("models/berkeley_varying.stan", dir = ".stancache") # the first model's priors, plus the prior on tau priors_varying <- c(priors, list(tau_sd = 0.5)) ``` ::: ### Step 7: Test on simulated data A new model needs the same test as the old one. This time the simulated world has the problem the posterior predictive check found: one department treats women differently. In this world, department A discriminates against women (−1 on the log-odds scale) and every other department treats men and women alike. We fit both models and compare them with the true value of the estimand. (A full second pass would also repeat the prior predictive check. We skip it here: the only new prior is the one on $\tau$.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sim_one_dept <- simulate_admissions(discrimination = c(-1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)) truth_one_dept <- true_direct_effect(sim_one_dept) recovery_varying <- list( "One sex effect" = fit_model(sim_one_dept), "A sex effect for each department" = fit_model(sim_one_dept, varying, priors_varying) ) |> map(\(f) direct_effect(f, data = sim_one_dept)) |> list_rbind(names_to = "model") |> mutate(model = fct_inorder(model)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} recovery_varying |> ggplot(aes(x = direct_effect, y = model)) + stat_halfeye(fill = BLUE) + geom_vline(xintercept = truth_one_dept, color = RED, linewidth = 1) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs( x = "Direct effect (female − male)", y = NULL, title = "Only department A discriminates", subtitle = "Red line: the true value of the estimand" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/recovery_varying_plot-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The true direct effect in this world is −5.2 points: department A admits women much less often, and about a fifth of all applicants apply there. The first model puts it at −3.1, missing a large part of it, because it lets department A count only as much as its few women allow. The new model puts it at −4.5, close to the truth: it estimates department A's effect from department A's applicants, and the estimand then counts that department as much as it should. Its posterior is wider, too. Estimating a sex effect for each department costs precision, and that's the honest price of not assuming the effects are equal. ### Step 8: Fit and check ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_varying <- fit_model(df, varying, priors_varying) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_varying$diagnostic_summary() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $num_divergent [1] 0 0 0 0 $num_max_treedepth [1] 0 0 0 0 $ebfmi [1] 0.7575906 0.7743792 0.6859522 0.8105267 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fit_varying$draws() |> subset_draws(variable = c("beta_bar", "tau", "beta")) |> summarise_draws() |> replace_indexes(df, beta_bar[sex], beta[sex, dept]) |> print(n = Inf, width = Inf) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 15 × 10 variable mean median sd mad q5 q95 rhat ess_bulk 1 beta_bar[male] -0.0801 -0.0791 0.116 0.103 -0.263 0.103 1.00 1311. 2 beta_bar[female] 0.0801 0.0791 0.116 0.103 -0.103 0.263 1.00 1311. 3 tau 0.239 0.215 0.118 0.0969 0.0908 0.464 1.00 992. 4 beta[male,A] -0.392 -0.392 0.136 0.137 -0.617 -0.170 1.00 1545. 5 beta[female,A] 0.392 0.392 0.136 0.137 0.170 0.617 1.00 1545. 6 beta[male,B] -0.0782 -0.0757 0.159 0.153 -0.348 0.173 1.000 1889. 7 beta[female,B] 0.0782 0.0757 0.159 0.153 -0.173 0.348 1.000 1889. 8 beta[male,C] 0.0430 0.0425 0.0712 0.0709 -0.0719 0.161 1.00 4608. 9 beta[female,C] -0.0430 -0.0425 0.0712 0.0709 -0.161 0.0719 1.00 4608. 10 beta[male,D] -0.0477 -0.0482 0.0704 0.0699 -0.165 0.0676 1.00 5442. 11 beta[female,D] 0.0477 0.0482 0.0704 0.0699 -0.0676 0.165 1.00 5442. 12 beta[male,E] 0.0607 0.0611 0.0988 0.101 -0.0970 0.223 1.00 3987. 13 beta[female,E] -0.0607 -0.0611 0.0988 0.101 -0.223 0.0970 1.00 3987. 14 beta[male,F] -0.0894 -0.0882 0.126 0.120 -0.298 0.116 1.00 4677. 15 beta[female,F] 0.0894 0.0882 0.126 0.120 -0.116 0.298 1.00 4677. ess_tail 1 1956. 2 1956. 3 875. 4 1159. 5 1159. 6 1906. 7 1906. 8 3345. 9 3345. 10 3697. 11 3697. 12 3428. 13 3428. 14 3308. 15 3308. ``` ::: ::: No divergences, $\hat{R}$ at 1 and ESS above a thousand: the sampler worked. The spread $\tau$ is clearly above zero, so the departments do differ. Department A stands out: its sex effect is the only one whose interval sits well away from zero. In the other departments, the effects are small and close to the average. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ppc_plot(fit_varying, "Posterior predictive check: a sex effect for each department") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/ppc_varying-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Every observed rate now falls inside its predicted interval, department A included. ## Step 9: Compute the estimate Now we can answer the question from Step 1. We compute the direct effect for every posterior draw of the second model. To see what the second pass changed, we compute it from the first model too, and, for the choice we made in Step 3, averaged over the women who applied instead of over all applicants: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} de <- direct_effect(fit_varying) estimates <- list( "First model: one sex effect" = direct_effect(fit), "Second model: a sex effect for each department" = de, "Second model, averaged over women applicants" = direct_effect(fit_varying, weight_by = filter(df, sex == "female")) ) |> list_rbind(names_to = "estimate") |> mutate(estimate = fct_rev(fct_inorder(estimate))) estimates |> ggplot(aes(x = direct_effect, y = estimate)) + stat_halfeye(fill = BLUE) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs( x = "Direct effect (female − male)", y = NULL, title = "Posterior for the estimand" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/estimand-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_summary <- estimates |> group_by(estimate) |> summarise( median = median(direct_effect), lower_90 = quantile(direct_effect, 0.05), upper_90 = quantile(direct_effect, 0.95), prob_women_disadvantaged = mean(direct_effect < 0) ) |> arrange(desc(estimate)) estimate_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Among applicants to the same department, there's no sign that women are admitted less often than men. With a sex effect for each department, the estimate is +3.5 percentage points: being seen as a woman *raises* an applicant's chance of admission, by between +0.7 and +6.4 points (90% interval). The probability that women are disadvantaged is 2%. The first model said +1.8. It understated the advantage for the same reason it understated the discrimination in the Step 7 simulation: it gave department A too little weight. That advantage comes almost entirely from department A. Averaged over the women who applied, most of them to departments C–F, the effect is +0.5 points (−2.2 to +3.1): no difference either way. This is the choice from Step 3, and here it matters. We committed to averaging over all applicants, so our estimate stays +3.5. But a reader who cares about the women who actually applied should know that, for them, the answer is "no difference". The two versions agree on the question we started with: departments don't treat women worse than the men who apply alongside them. Compare that with the overall gap: women were admitted 14 percentage points less often than men. That gap comes from *where* women apply, not from how departments treat them. That's the pattern our Step 4 simulation produced in a world with no discrimination. ## Step 10: Test its robustness A result is only as good as the assumptions behind it, so we test how much it depends on them. ### Sensitivity to priors We refit the second model with different priors: the baseline and department priors ($\alpha$, $\gamma$), which Step 7 found too wide, at half and twice their width; the sex-effect priors ($\bar\beta$, $\tau$) at twice their width; and sex-effect priors so narrow that they all but rule out any difference between men and women. Because the prior scales are data, each variant is the same model with different numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_scenarios <- list( "Default priors" = list(), "α, γ priors half as wide" = list(alpha_sd = 0.75, gamma_sd = 0.5), "α, γ priors twice as wide" = list(alpha_sd = 3, gamma_sd = 2), "Sex-effect priors twice as wide" = list(beta_sd = 2, tau_sd = 1), "Sex-effect priors insisting on no effect" = list(beta_sd = 0.02, tau_sd = 0.02) ) prior_sensitivity <- prior_scenarios |> imap(\(change, name) { fit_model(df, varying, modifyList(priors_varying, change)) |> direct_effect() |> mutate(scenario = name) }) |> list_rbind() |> mutate(scenario = fct_rev(fct_inorder(scenario))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_sensitivity |> ggplot(aes(x = direct_effect, y = scenario)) + stat_halfeye(fill = BLUE) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs( x = "Direct effect (female − male)", y = NULL, title = "Sensitivity to priors" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/sensitivity_priors_plot-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Making the baseline and department priors narrower or wider barely moves the estimate, and neither does widening the sex-effect priors: across those four fits, the median runs from +2.7 to +3.7 points. This confirms what we expected in Step 7: with thousands of applicants, the data outweigh the overly wide priors. Only the last prior moves it, to +0.5 points. That prior says, before seeing any data, that no department's sex effect can be more than a few hundredths on the log-odds scale. It overrides department A's data because that's what it was built to do. No one holds that belief, so it doesn't weaken the result. What it shows is that the advantage for women rests on department A's applicants, and that it takes a prior ruling such a difference out in advance to remove it. ### Sensitivity to the DAG: an unobserved confounder The strongest assumption we made is that, within each department, the men and women who apply are equally qualified. Step 2 gave two ways it could fail. Here they are in the DAG, with qualifications as `U`, a variable we can't observe, and with `Applied`, which we condition on because the data hold only people who applied:
dag { Admitted [outcome,pos=\"2,0\"] Applied [adjusted,pos=\"0.4,1.6\"] Department [adjusted,pos=\"1,0.7\"] Sex [exposure,pos=\"0,0\"] U [latent,pos=\"1.6,1.6\"] Department -> Admitted Sex -> Admitted Sex -> Applied Sex -> Department U -> Admitted U -> Applied U -> Department }
- **Selection into applying** ($\text{Sex} \to \text{Applied} \leftarrow U$). Suppose women face barriers *before* they apply, so only the most qualified women apply at all. Then, within any department, the women are more qualified than the men. Comparing within departments would make women look favored even if departments discriminate against them. - **Qualifications drive where people apply** ($\text{Sex} \to \text{Department} \leftarrow U$). If strong applicants aim for the selective departments, then a man in a selective department is more likely to be a strong applicant than a woman there, since women apply to those departments anyway. Comparing within departments would make women look *disadvantaged*, even with no discrimination. In both cases, the path runs through a variable we hold fixed, and holding it fixed is what makes men and women differ in `U`. We can test how much this matters by going back to the Step 4 simulation and adding `U`. Everything else stays the same. The new lines are marked. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} simulate_admissions_u <- function( n = 4500, discrimination = 0, # Sex -> Admitted: effect of being female, in log-odds depts = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"), admit_rate = c(0.65, 0.60, 0.35, 0.33, 0.25, 0.07), # Department -> Admitted male_pref = c(0.31, 0.21, 0.12, 0.15, 0.07, 0.14), # Sex -> Department female_pref = c(0.06, 0.02, 0.32, 0.20, 0.21, 0.19), # Sex -> Department u_on_admit = 0, # new: how much qualifications matter for admission female_selection = 0, # new: how much more qualified female applicants are, in SDs u_on_dept = 0 # new: how strongly qualified applicants aim for selective departments ) { # one row per department (single values are recycled to every department) departments <- tibble( dept = fct(depts), discrimination, admit_rate, male_pref, female_pref ) # Sex: 60% men, as in the real data sex <- sample(fct(c("male", "female")), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.6, 0.4)) # new: qualifications, shifted up for women when female_selection > 0 u <- rnorm(n, mean = female_selection * (sex == "female")) # Sex, Qualifications -> Department (new: the tilt toward selective departments) selectivity <- -qlogis(departments$admit_rate) selectivity <- selectivity - mean(selectivity) dept <- map2_vec(sex, u, \(s, u_i) { pref <- if (s == "female") departments$female_pref else departments$male_pref sample(departments$dept, 1, prob = pref * exp(u_on_dept * u_i * selectivity)) }) # Department, Sex, Qualifications -> Admitted d <- match(dept, departments$dept) dept_rate <- departments$admit_rate[d] dept_discrimination <- departments$discrimination[d] log_odds <- qlogis(dept_rate) + dept_discrimination * (sex == "female") + u_on_admit * u # new admitted <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(log_odds)) tibble(dept, sex, dept_rate, dept_discrimination, u, admitted) } # the true direct effect now holds each applicant's qualifications fixed too true_direct_effect_u <- function(sim, u_on_admit) { log_odds_male <- qlogis(sim$dept_rate) + u_on_admit * sim$u # new log_odds_female <- log_odds_male + sim$dept_discrimination mean(plogis(log_odds_female) - plogis(log_odds_male)) } ``` ::: Now we build in real discrimination (−0.5 log-odds) in every department, make qualifications matter for admission, and try each failure in turn: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} confounding <- tribble( ~world, ~female_selection, ~u_on_dept, "Equally qualified", 0, 0, "Women 0.5 SD more qualified", 0.5, 0, "Women 1 SD more qualified", 1, 0, "Qualified aim for selective depts", 0, 1 ) |> mutate( world = fct_rev(fct_inorder(world)), sim = map2(female_selection, u_on_dept, \(k, t) { simulate_admissions_u( discrimination = -0.5, u_on_admit = 1, female_selection = k, u_on_dept = t ) }), truth = map_dbl(sim, \(s) true_direct_effect_u(s, u_on_admit = 1)), estimate = map(sim, \(s) { direct_effect(fit_model(s, varying, priors_varying), data = s) }) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} confounding |> select(world, truth, estimate) |> unnest(estimate) |> ggplot(aes(x = direct_effect, y = world)) + stat_halfeye(fill = BLUE) + geom_point( data = distinct(confounding, world, truth), aes(x = truth), color = RED, shape = 4, size = 4, stroke = 1.5 ) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + geom_vline( xintercept = median(de$direct_effect), color = BLUE, linetype = "dotted" ) + labs( x = "Estimated direct effect (female − male)", y = NULL, title = "Real discrimination, distorted by an unobserved confounder", subtitle = "Red ×: true effect. Dotted line: our estimate from the real data." ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](workflow_files/figure-html/sensitivity_confounding_plot-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: In every one of these worlds, departments discriminate against women (red ×). When men and women are equally qualified, the model finds the discrimination. The two failures from Step 2 push the estimate in opposite directions. If women applicants are half a standard deviation more qualified, the discrimination vanishes from the estimate, and at a full standard deviation women look clearly *favored*, by more than our real-data estimate (dotted line). If qualified applicants aim for the selective departments, the model finds *more* discrimination than there is. So our real-data result is credible only to the extent that we believe the men and women who apply to the same department are similarly qualified. If they aren't, the error could go either way, and how far depends on which story is true. The model can't settle that question. It's an argument about the world, and settling it would take more data, such as measures of applicant qualifications. # The result Within departments, we find no evidence that women are disadvantaged, at least in the six departments in our data. Averaged over all applicants, as we decided in Step 3, being seen as a woman raises the chance of admission by +3.5 percentage points, almost all of it in department A. Averaged over the women who actually applied, there is no difference. The conclusion holds up across a range of priors, and only a prior that rules out any sex effect in advance removes the advantage. It rests on an assumption we can't test with these data: that men and women who apply to the same department are similarly qualified. If that's wrong, the error could go either way. The overall gap is real: women were admitted 14 percentage points less often than men. It runs through department choice, so the place to look is why women apply to more selective departments.
